Mechatronics capstone / Fleming College / 2023–2024

Power of
Induction.

From a supplied concept to a working bench prototype. I took the lead on hands-on development, bringing the heating electronics, water circuit, and temperature monitoring together.

It took assembly, fault finding, and a few revisions to get there. The result: a demonstrated rise in outlet temperature, and a clear understanding of what the next version needed.

A bench demonstration of startup heating response. Flow rate, input power, and heating efficiency were not quantified.

01 / My contribution

I carried the build
through the details.

This was a team capstone, and I carried most of the hands-on implementation. My work spanned wiring and soldering, prototype assembly and fabrication, insulation checks, leak troubleshooting, testing, and technical documentation.

I integrated purchased heating and temperature-monitoring modules into a bench setup, investigated unwanted electrical contact in the coil assembly, and demonstrated the heating response. The practical challenge was making the electrical and fluid systems work together.

The project brief and original mechanical concept came from sponsor Cole Radoja. My focus here is the implementation, troubleshooting, and test work I carried out.

The water warmed up. The electronics got a little too enthusiastic. That gave me the next problem to solve.

02 / The starting point

A concept with several systems to connect.

The brief explored fluid heating using an induction module and a steel insert within copper tubing. It also proposed temperature-controlled switching and a future magnetocaloric cooling system.

The concept brought a reservoir, pump, electronics supports, and fluid connections into one package. During development, the immediate priority became assembling and testing the heating subsystem.

What reached the bench

  • An AC–DC supply powering the ZVS induction-heating module.
  • A pump feeding water through tubing and the coil into a separate collection container.
  • An outlet temperature probe connected to a W1209 display.
  • A manual power switch and an external cooling fan.

Within the academic project timeframe, development focused on the heating demonstration. The integrated enclosure and magnetocaloric cooling system remained unfinished.

03 / Development & troubleshooting

The useful work happened between tests.

01 / Electrical isolation

Find the unintended contact.

Continuity checks identified electrical contact between the steel insert and copper tube. I added insulation and checked the revised assembly. The meter then indicated an open circuit between the two under the test conditions.

02 / Fluid connections

Get the water through the coil.

Fitting and tubing connections needed attention during assembly. I worked through the leak points and applied sealant at the tube-to-coil joints before demonstrating the pumped heating setup.

03 / Thermal management

Watch the hardware, too.

I used a fan to cool the heating board and monitored the outlet reading during manual operation. Board overheating still limited the run, making cooling and controlled switching priorities for a future revision.

04 / Demonstration

A measurable response at the outlet.

I started the fan and water pump, recorded the initial outlet-sensor reading, and switched on the heating module. Water passed through the coil to a separate collection container while I watched the temperature rise.

Observed outcome

A 21.1°C rise in the outlet reading.

The demonstration narration reports approximately 40 seconds between the initial and final readings. The setup produced a clear heating response, with manual shutdown required because of board overheating.

These readings describe the outlet sensor during startup. They do not establish steady-state heating capacity, the temperature of all collected water, or energy efficiency. The original flow and temperature targets were not validated.

05 / Proposed control development

From manual switching to a closed loop.

The next development goal would be automatic regulation of outlet water temperature. In the demonstration I monitored the display and operated the switch myself. A closed loop controller would compare the measured outlet temperature with a selected setpoint and adjust heating power.

Measure

Temperature and flow.

Use a calibrated outlet probe in a consistent position, measure inlet temperature and actual flow, and log the response. Check board temperature separately so water-temperature control cannot hide electronics overheating.

Control

Start simple. Tune from tests.

First establish stable operation with on/off control and hysteresis. Evaluate PI control for smoother regulation and reduced steady-state error. Add derivative action only if the measured response justifies it.

Actuate

A compatible power stage.

Use a heater with a documented control input, or validate a properly rated switching interface for the existing module. An emergency stop, loss-of-flow shutdown, and independent overtemperature protection would override normal control.

Proposed next iteration, not implemented in the demonstrated prototype. A generic resonant ZVS board must not be assumed compatible with rapid supply switching or PWM.

How I would evaluate PI or PID control

At a known, stable flow, record a safe heating step test to identify the response speed and the delay between a power change and the outlet reading. Start with conservative PI settings, constrain the output to the available power, and prevent integral windup when the command saturates or heating is disabled.

Assess setpoint tracking, overshoot, settling time, and recovery after controlled changes in inlet temperature or flow. Derivative action would be considered only if it improves performance without amplifying measurement noise. A closed loop can regulate an achievable setpoint; it cannot compensate for insufficient heating power.

06 / Engineering reflection

What worked. What I would change.

What the prototype established

  • Integration of the power supply, purchased heating module, pump, fluid connections, and temperature display.
  • A documented approach to diagnosing unwanted electrical contact and checking the insulation change.
  • A demonstrated outlet-temperature rise in a single-pass bench setup.
  • Identification of thermal limitations that prevented sustained operation.

Priorities for another iteration

  • Measure actual flow, supply voltage/current, and both inlet and outlet temperatures over repeated tests.
  • Improve board cooling and introduce appropriately rated automatic power switching with independent overtemperature protection.
  • Verify insulation and sealing materials for the actual temperature and fluid-contact conditions.
  • Set achievable flow and temperature targets from the available power before pursuing the packaged system.
A closer look at the design targets

The early specification paired a target of 200 L/hour with a 50–100°C heating range. Heating water from 21.9°C to 50°C at 200 L/hour would require approximately 6.5 kW before losses. The listed 24 V, 42 A supply provides about 1 kW, so those simultaneous single-pass targets exceeded the available power.

The demonstration's actual flow rate was not measured. A future test would establish the achievable temperature rise at a known flow. A relay or transistor switching stage could automate operation; it would not increase the power available from the supply.

Magnetocaloric cooling remained part of the original research scope, with no cooling prototype demonstrated.

07 / What I take forward

Build it. Measure it. Improve it.

This project brought electrical assembly, fluid handling, and testing into the same problem. I carried the practical work forward, documented the response, and identified the changes needed for a more controlled, repeatable system.

Next iteration: planned. Budget: pending. Ideas—and sponsors—welcome.
